newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek court approves extradition of German woman.
newsitem.headline: Greek court approves extradition of German woman.

text.p: A Greek appeals court has approved the extradition of a woman wanted in Germany in connection with a 1986 West Berlin disco bombing that killed three people and wounded 200, court officials said on Wednesday.
The woman, identified as Andrea Hausler, was arrested while vacationing in northern Greece in October with her two-year-old son and a male friend.
Greek police have said that Hausler is the sister of a key suspect in the disco bombing, in which scores of off-duty U.S. military personnel were hurt.
Two U.S. soldiers and a Turkish woman were killed in the attack, which prompted a U.S. air strike against Libya.
Court officials said there were no charges against Hausler in Greece and she would probably leave soon for Germany.
Socialist Justice Minister Evangelos Yannopoulos will have the final say and must sign her extradition order. Officials said Tuesday's court recommendation had not reached Athens.

On a number of past occasions In the past, Greece's socialist governments have refused to extradite guerrilla suspects for what were deemed politically motivated crimes and this was seen as a test case for new Prime Minister Costas Simitis.
Hausler is the sister of a woman identified as Verena C., 37, who was detained in Berlin in early October and accused of planting the bomb in the disco.
German prosecutors have given no details on what role they believe Hausler might have played in the bombing.
Berlin prosecutors arrested Verena C. and her Palestinian ex-husband, Ali C., saying she was suspected of planting the deadly bomb at his request.

The United States blamed Libya for the attack on the "La Belle" disco and responded by bombing the Arab state, killing at least 15 people, including an adopted 15-month-old daughter of leader Muammar Gaddafi and wounding more than 100.
German prosecutors said they believed Verena C. had planted the bomb at the request of Ali C. and another suspect, Yasser Shraydi, who was extradited to Germany from Lebanon in May this year.
They believe the attack was orchestrated from the Libyan embassy in East Berlin.

They have also issued arrest warrants for three former members of the Libyan embassy in East Berlin -- identified only by the surnames Elamin, Keshlaf and Al Abani -- and a Libyan secret service member named Rashed.
The prosecutors believe those suspects provided the explosives and helped organise the bombing but that they are now back in their homeland.
